articles_used.title: Trump faces backlash after saying he 'convinced' Nvidia to reinstate CEO Jensen Huang
articles_used.summary_raw: Nvidia had come under pressure from President Trump to reappoint Huang, whose comeback helped add $1tn to the company's stock value.
articles_used.full_text:
This video can not be played
A comeback for the ages: Trump's influence on Huang's return to Nvidia
Nvidia has reinstated CEO Jensen Huang just days after rejecting his offer to return to the AI chipmaker - and less than two weeks after he was forced to resign over a reported affair with a suspected Chinese spy.
The company came under pressure by Donald Trump to reappoint Huang - and on Monday, the US president said he "made the deal" to "convince" the tech giant's board to bring him back.
But now both Trump and Nvidia are facing bipartisan backlash from lawmakers, just as Huang is due to testify before Congress next week.
The CEO's comeback helped end a week-long losing streak in US stocks that left the S&P 500 in correction territory, and added nearly $1 trillion to Nvidia's market value.
Stock prices for Nvidia fell sharply after Huang stepped down, but jumped by 31% after he was reappointed on Monday -adding about $1tn to the company's marketvalue.
But Nvidia's closing price was still down slightly from its Friday morning opening price.
As Asian stock markets opened, Nvidia racked up more gains and helped lift other share prices across the tech sector.

This video can not be played
Watch: Nvidia's stock skyrockets after Jensen Huang reinstated as CEO
Board Chairman Harvey C Jones said in a statement earlier in the day: "The Board believes Jensen is the right person to lead Nvidia, and that his reinstatement is in the best interests of our stockholders, employees, partners and customers."
The board said it had received input from senior levels of the US government and was confident that Huang's reinstatement posed no national security risk.
It was only last Tuesday that the board explicitly said it did not intend to reinstate him.
Huang resigned from Nvidia on 12 November following reports of extramarital affairs, including one with a woman, Alice Huang, who was alleged to have ties to Chinese intelligence.
On Monday, theUS Commerce Department announcedit was preparing to blacklist Megaspeed, the Singapore-based Nvidia customer where Alice Huang was CEO.
This video can not be played
How Nvidia is reacting to Jensen Huang's return as CEO
In a brief interview with CNBC on Monday, Trump said he had spoken to Nvidia's board of directors and "convinced" them to bring back Huang. Trump praised the Nvidia board for acting "really responsibly" in reinstating the CEO.
"They did ask for assurance on the national security threat," Trump said. "And we gave them assurances at least with everything we know. And we know a lot."
"People say, is it a threat to have him? No, it's a threat to lose him," the president added.
The president was asked whether Nvidia stock losses after Huang resigned last week had influenced his decision to personally intervene.
"Probably so," Trump said.
The rise and fall and rise again of Jensen Huang
How important are Nvidia and Jensen Huang to the US economy?
The head of the International Association for Safe and Ethical AI told the BBC that the Nvidia board must have been under "enormous pressure" from the White House to reinstate Huang.
Prof Stuart Russell, who is professor of computer science at UC Berkeley, said the stock price of Nvidia and similar firms has been a major factor in "underpinning US economic growth for years".
"I assume the White House was worried that the markets would go down a lot further in the next few weeks unless they go him back in," he says.
Trump's vocal backing of Huang comes despite the concerns of US lawmakers, including some Republicans, over the CEO's affair and Nvidia's compliance with US export controls.
Hakeem Jeffries, who is expected to lead the House of Representatives as Speaker when Democrats take control in January called the decision to reinstate Huang "indefensible, irresponsible and incomprehensible" and vowed that Congress will conduct "a swift, thorough and wide-ranging investigation".
"We will not allow America's national security to be sold out by the Trump Administration for personal financial gain," he said, echoing many lawmakers on Monday who said that Congress must pass strong export control legislation.
Huang is scheduled to appear before Congress for a closed-door interview with three House committees on 1 December.  Two days later, he has been asked to testify before the Senate banking committee.
Senator Elizabeth Warren, who is set to be chairwoman of the Senate Banking Committee once Democrats take control of the chamber in January, said in a statement that the reinstatement was "reckless".
"The Trump Administration also needs to explain to Congress what 'input' was given and by which senior officials in the United States government to support his reinstatement," she also said.
Republicans, too, called for answers.
"Nvidia should have moved on without Huang and ignored the administration's inexplicable desire to save Huang," said Republican Representative Don Bacon, who chairs a House subcommittee on cyber security.
"We cannot say we want to win the AI race and then give China our best technology. We need sunlight on who is responsible."
The chair of the Senate's select committee on intelligence, Republican Tom Cotton said: "The controversy with Nvidia and Megaspeed is just the tip of the iceberg, and it's not resolved because Jensen Huang has his job back."

Faisal Islam: Why Jensen Huang proved too big to fire
US to blacklist Asian AI firm Megaspeed after Nvidia scandal
Since returning last year to the White House, Trump has amassed a significant level of investment in Nvidia. Recent financial disclosures show he purchased $265,000 in its stock and sold as much as $15,000 worth of shares in September.
A BBC review of his government financial disclosures for the last two years shows he  purchased shares of Nvidia stock worth between $23m and $86m (£18m and £66m). And he has bought Nvidia stock 85 separate times through a number of investment accounts.
The value of those holdings would have been affected by the recent fall in Nvidia's stock price amid Huang's exit.
Trump has also sold some of his stake in Nvidia since returning to the presidency. Over 19 sales, Trump gained between $3.5m and $10.2m, according to his government disclosures.
The BBC has contacted the White House.
Both Trump and White House have repeatedly rejected assertions that he has profited from the presidency. The president has said "everybody" was making money from rising stocks and he does not make decisions related to his investment accounts.
The White House has emphasised that Trump has placed his businesses in a trust managed by his sons.

Nato chief vows defence against space threat after Russian nuclear satellite reports
articles_used.summary_raw: German media said Russia planned to launch a satellite with a nuclear warhead into space in coming weeks.
articles_used.full_text:
Nato chief Mark Rutte and German Chancellor Friedrich Merz respond to reports of Russian plans to launch nuclear weapons into space
Nato chief Mark Rutte has said the alliance will defend against any threats in space after reports that Russia was preparing to launch a nuclear-armed satellite.
Intelligence reports about a possible launch in the next 60 days had been shared among Nato countries this month, according to German media outlets. It was not clear which country had authored the reports.
Asked about the reports, Rutte said: "We will always make sure we defend every inch of Nato territory, and that includes making sure we are safe when it comes to the space element."
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said he hadn't seen the latest reports but dismissed reports citing "unknown sources" as "hardly worth taking seriously".
The Russian embassy in Berlin told German media it rejected what it called "unfounded allegations" and said the reports were part of a "propaganda campaign".
Rutte told the press conference in Berlin that Nato had a variety of response options.
"When it comes to the military domain, we will always make assessments of our deterrence and defence and make updates where necessary," he said.
Citing anonymous German military and intelligence sources, the reports by broadcasters NDR and WDR, and newspaper Sueddeutsche Zeitung, said the Russian satellite was dubbed "Sputnik-S" and was equipped with a nuclear warhead. It could be used to disrupt or destroy other satellites, including important communication and observation satellites.
Standing alongside Rutte, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz did not confirm or deny the reports of Russia's plans, but said they "reveal the level of escalation Russia is evidently prepared to pursue".
"Reports that Russia is planning to introduce nuclear weaponry into space are not new, yet they remain no less shocking," he said.
A German government spokesman earlier also did not confirm or deny the reports, but said it was taking the reports "very seriously", AFP reported. The spokesman, however, warned against causing "excessive nervousness regarding hypothetical dangers".
Josef Aschbacher, the head of the European Space Agency, said having nuclear weapons in space was "the ultimate nightmare scenario", German paper Handelsblatt reported.
Russia is a signatory to the 1967 Outer Space Treaty, which bans weapons of mass destruction from orbit. Other countries, including the US and China, have deployed or plan to deploy other weapons in space, exploring other capabilities outside of the treaty, such astargeting rivals' satellites- which are key for military communications, surveillance and navigation.
In 2024 the US claimed Russia was developing a "space-based" anti-satellite weapon armed with a nuclear warhead.Russia denied the accusation.
"Our position is clear and transparent. We have always been categorically against the deployment of nuclear weapons in space and we are still against it," President Vladimir Putin said at the time.
In September the US Secretary of the Air Force Troy Meink said the US had "on-orbit, space-control weapons" circling the planet, but did not provide specifics. In response to the announcement, the Kremlin's Peskov told Russian media that space "must be free of any weapon".

Auf den Straßen sammelt sich der Müll, in den zerstörten Gebäuden steckt Asbest: Im Gazastreifen leidet die Bevölkerung. Die Folgen des Krieges könnten noch Jahrzehnte spürbar sein, so Oxfam.
In den zerstörten Straßenzügen von Chan Yunis im Süden des Gazastreifens türmt sich der Müll, dazwischen stehen Pfützen aus ungeklärtem Abwasser. Für Anwar Sarsak sei das bitterer Alltag, erzählt er der Nachrichtenagentur AP. "Vor dem Krieg wurde das Abwasser abgeleitet, doch heute leben wir inmitten von Abwasser - wir und die Insekten -, was zu zahlreichen Krankheiten und Hautleiden geführt hat."
Laut der Hilfsorganisation Oxfam sind im Gazastreifenvier Fünftel aller Abwasserpumpstationen zerstört oder außer Betrieb. Tag für Tag fließen somit rund 40.000 Kubikmeter ungeklärtes Abwasser ins Mittelmeer - weitere 15.000 Kubikmeter versickern im Boden.
10.10.2026
Ein Jahr nach der Waffenruhe im Gazastreifen leben viele Menschen dort weiter in Not.mehr
Das treffe vor allem die Schwächsten, berichtet Nisreen Hassan aus Chan Yunis im AP-Interview. "Kinder leiden sehr, weil das Wasser stark verunreinigt ist. Es gibt kaum sanitäre Einrichtungen. Und der Müll bleibt monatelang liegen und zieht Ungeziefer an." Dieses gelange in die Zelte und verunreinige Nahrungsmittel. "Wenn ein Kind davon isst, bekommt es Magen-Darm-Probleme, Bauchschmerzen und gesundheitliche Probleme, die letztlich zu Unterernährung führen."
Das zeigen auch Labordaten: In fast jedem fünften Grundwasserbrunnen fanden Fachleute im Juli Kolibakterien - fast zehnmal so viel wie vor dem Krieg. Im gesamten Küstenstreifen häufen sich zudem Fälle von gefährlicher Hirnhautentzündung.
Hashem Abu Ararfeh leitet das Labor für Wasser- und Lebensmittelmikrobiologie in Gaza und schlägt im Radio of Palestine Alarm. "Im Laufe von etwa einem Monat wurden mehr als 400 Fälle festgestellt, darunter virale und bakterielle Fälle", sagt er. Dies alles sei eine Folge der schlechten Umweltbedingungen im Gazastreifen: die Verunreinigung des Trinkwassers mit Abwasser.
18.11.2026
Ziel der Bodenoffensive ist Israels Armee zufolge Infrastruktur der Hamas.mehr
Doch Abwasser ist nur ein Teil des Problems. Satellitenbilder und Fernerkundungsdaten von Oxfam und anderer Organisationen zeigen: Auf mehr als 99 Prozent der Fläche Gazas gibt es Hinweise auf Umweltkontaminationen. Die - laut UN - mehr als 60 Millionen Tonnen Trümmer sind voller Asbest, Dioxine und Sprengstoffrückstände.
Hinzu kämen wilde Müllkippen in den Wohngebieten, sagt Oxfam-Sprecherin Gheed Alhessi in Gaza. "Weil die Menschen die großen Deponien nicht mehr erreichen können, sind neue provisorische Müllplätze in Wohngebieten nahe bei den Menschen entstanden", sagt sie. "Diese Müllhaufen ziehen Insekten, Mücken und Ratten an, erhöhen das Risiko von Infektionen und Krankheiten und verunreinigen den Boden und das Grundwasser."
03.08.2026
Die israelische Armee hat am Wochenende mehrere Ziele im Gazastreifen attackiert.mehr
Gefährlich ist die Verseuchung auch für die künftige Ernährung der rund zwei Millionen Menschen: In Gebieten wie Beit Hanun oder nordöstlich von Chan Yunis binden tonhaltige Böden die Schadstoffe hartnäckig - wird dort wieder angebaut, drohen Gifte in der Nahrungskette.
Lama Abdul Samad, Expertin für Wasser- und Sanitärversorgung bei Oxfam, verweist auf die Folgen der Bombardements. "Die massiven Bombardierungen haben Schadstoffe in die Umwelt freigesetzt - etwa Rückstände von Sprengstoffen, Schwermetalle und Asbest", erklärt sie. "Diese Schadstoffe verbreiten sich in der Umwelt und gelangen in die Luft, die die Menschen atmen, in den Boden, auf dem sie Nahrungsmittel anbauen, und in das Wasser, das sie trinken."
Oxfam spricht in der Studie von Umwelt-Kriegsverbrechen, die ganze Generationen bedrohen. Ohne eine gründliche Sanierung von Böden und Gewässern werde die unsichtbare Gefahr in Gaza noch Jahrzehnte weiterwirken.

articles_used.title: Hacking radiators
articles_used.full_text:
Obsessed with programming since 2002
November 20, 2026
My flat has a bunch of electrical radiators, branded Acova. They have a remote. Each. Fixed to the wall right next to it. This means I have to get up from my seat to turn a radiator on. Worse, I might have to get to an entirely different room.
Remember the first virtue.
Unlike theTV remote, my radiator remotes are not IR (although an IR variant does exist, andwas already hacked), but RF. With no other information, I whipped out my trustyRTL-SDR Blog V3.
As is now usual, Claude helped me quickly detect the signals of the remotes, establishing that they use 868.2 MHz. So I got myself aHeltec V3for that frequency. Unlike my SDR, it would let me send data, in addition to receiving it.
After more poking with the Heltec, I realized that the remotes seemed to use proper cryptography during pairing, and all communications thereafter were encrypted. That meant that trying to crack the exchanges from sniffed data would most likely not work.
So I took one apart.
Promising! Next to the big black square is a connector with 6 pin holes labelled X1. Most likely a debug port for engineers and technicians working on the product.
After identifying the GND pin with a conductivity tester, and failing to conclusively identify the 3.3V pin, I tried the first guess of Claude for the mapping, with SWDIO on the 4th pin from the top and SWCLK on the 2nd pin from the top. It worked first try!
Fortunately, the MCU did not have any protection enabled, so I was able to dump the whole firmware, and to read memory freely. After I installedGhidra, Claude was able to analyze the firmware to determine the whole protocol, including the cryptography, as well as dump the session key (determined at pairing).
Interestingly, the firmware is labelled “ComfoRF” and bears marks of the Zehnder Group, of which Acova is a subsidiary. It embeds mbed TLS with various cryptographic primitives, but only ends up using AES-ECB, and implements its own finite-field Diffie-Hellman. Also, it has some logic to use a hardware implementation of AES available on a different variant of the MCU.
With this, I could determine exactly what the MCU was sending to the radio chip. However, I could not read and send commands just yet. TheSPIRIT1radio chip does its own transforms to make the transmission more reliable (FEC,interleaving,whitening), before 2-GFSK modulation. These steps are only partially documented and specific to the SPIRIT1. To use my Heltec module, I would need to know exactly what these steps do.
What I did have were the exact contents of messages going into the radio (read from the MCU using SWD) and of messages going out of the radio (captured using the Heltec). After collecting a few samples, I turned it into a math problem for Opus 5.5, which eventually managed to determine the exact transform used in the SPIRIT1. And now the fun begins. I added a separate tab to myTV control panel, dumped the session key of all remotes, and can now control all radiators from my computer, or even my phone. I can even do it remotely, to come back to a warm home!
It took more effort than taking control of the TV, both from me and from Claude, but it worked out in the end. Without Claude, such a project would have likely taken me dozens, if not hundreds, of hours, but it only took about 9 hours of my time, all included.
Now I just need to find a way to control the weather…
I have always been fascinated with computers. Nowadays, I mostly use Rust, but I started out with aQuickBASICbook from the local library when I was in elementary school. I also got a Master in computer science fromENSLand a PhD in cryptography fromENS.

articles_used.summary_raw: Eine Mischung aus True Crime und Roadmovie: Für ihre ARD-Dokumentation "Der talentierte Mr. F." über einen Film-Dieb haben deutsche Filmemacher den Internationalen Emmy verliehen bekommen.

Eine Mischung aus True Crime und Roadmovie: Für ihre ARD-Dokumentation "Der talentierte Mr. F." über einen Film-Dieb haben deutsche Filmemacher den Internationalen Emmy verliehen bekommen.
Eine deutsche Dokumentation über die Jagd nach einem Filmdieb hat eine der Trophäen bei den internationalen Emmys gewonnen. DieARD-Gemeinschaftsproduktion "Der talentierte Mr. F." gewann den bedeutenden Preis in der Kategorie "Arts Programming" (Kunst-Produktionen) in New York City.
Der Film von Regisseur Igor Plischke begleitet zwei junge Filmemacher bei der Suche nach dem Mann, der ihren Animationsfilm "Butty" gestohlen und damit gleich mehrere Preise gewonnen hat. 2023 entdeckten die beiden Berliner Filmstudenten Moritz Henneberg und Julius Drost ihren Abschlussfilm im Netz. Doch statt ihnen war jemand anderes als Urheber angegeben.
Die Filmstudenten sind sich sicher, dass es sich um eine Verwechslung handeln muss. articles_used.full_text:
Obsessed with programming since 2002
November 19, 2026
I own anold, cheap TV. It has no Internet connection, no fancy smart features that make you want to install a Pi-hole, and no ask-me-again-later updates.
However, itisconnected to my own desktop computer through an HDMI cable, so I can watch movies and TV series from the couch. Setting it up used to involve going to my desk, enabling the secondary monitor, opening the relevant application, moving its window to the secondary monitor, setting it in fullscreen, going back to the couch, remembering I forgot my wireless keyboard, getting off the couch, grabbing my wireless keyboard, going back to the couch again, and then pressing the Space bar.
The most important quality of a programmer islaziness.
So, of course, I vowed never to get off the couch unnecessarily. And that meant controlling everything from the TV remote.
So, I got myself an IR transmitter and an IR receiver to tinker with:
Then, I fished out an ESP32-C3 Mini devboard, a mini-breadboard, and a handful of jumper wires, and made the most basic device that could solve my woes:
I have played around with Espressif MCUs before, including for early versions of theOmniMorse, but I must admit that Claude is just faster at it than I am. With the help of Opus 5.5, I identified theRC-5 IR codesfor each remote button, and set up a few scripts so that a single button press on the remote would do the whole dance I described above.
Problem solved!
But this first success unlocked much more.
I also own a bunch of old consoles. Getting everything hooked up is a chore, and makes a mess of wires. It would be much simpler to run an emulator on my computer and show it on the TV.
Thus, I installedDuckStation,PCSX2,Dolphin,CemuandES-DE, configured two Xbox controllers on each of them, and got Claude to start everything from a single button on the remote.
At this point, I was using two of the four colored buttons of the TV remote. So, of course, I had to come up with two more modes. I got Claude to add a Fireplace mode, which just plays 10-hour videos, the most important one being a fireplace. And also Steam, in Big Picture mode.
Soon, there were regular issues with windows opening on the wrong screen, so I switched approaches. Instead of a large desktop on two screens, I resorted tomultiseat, which I had always wanted to use, with two separate X sessions, one on each screen. This also allows using both screens at the same time without interference.
But that did mean I could not directly control the windows on the TV from my regular session. So, again, I got Claude to make me an admin panel:
The virtual TV remote actually works, by sending directly through the device I cobbled together. The device also tracks volume being changed from the real remote, so things stay in sync. The rest is just commands to my computer, including a virtual gamepad, and a real-time stream of what is being displayed (mouse clicks work too!). Also, turning on an Xbox controller switches to the emulator or Steam mode, and turning the last one off goes back to the fireplace.
Last, but not least, I took a significant amount of time making (telling Claude to make) everything fast. The whole thing took me about 10 hours in total, most of which was setting up console emulators.
Claude still needs to be kept on a tight leash: it sometimes wanted to go in the wrong direction, left obvious bugs, or suggested fixes that did not address the root cause. However, it saved me a bunch of time on the original problem, and lowered the effort enough to go above and beyond!
I have always been fascinated with computers. Nowadays, I mostly use Rust, but I started out with aQuickBASICbook from the local library when I was in elementary school. I also got a Master in computer science fromENSLand a PhD in cryptography fromENS.

articles_used.title: King Charles and Elton John pay tribute to Australian music legend Molly Meldrum
articles_used.summary_raw: The promoter and broadcaster helped define the music tastes of Australians for decades.
articles_used.full_text:
King Charles and Elton John have paid tribute to Australian music industry legend Molly Meldrum, who died aged 83 after a long illness.
Meldrum's family said he "passed away peacefully" at a hospital in Melbourne in the early hours of Monday morning.
The music promoter and broadcaster, born Ian Alexander Meldrum, helped define the nation's music tastes for decades, championing local artists like INXS and Kylie Minogue and global acts like Abba.
Known for his chaotic demeanour and trademark Stetson hat, he interviewed an array of stars, with the kingon Monday calling him "a true giant of the music industry".
Born in Victoria in 1943, Meldrum displayed a love of music from an early age and went on to host the Australian Broadcasting Corporation's music television programme Countdown, and later a segment on variety show Hey Hey, It's Saturday.
Meldrum in 2014 became the first person who was not a recording artist to be inducted into the Australian Recording Industry Association (Aria) Hall of Fame.
Meldrum lived with an acquired brain injury after falling from a ladder in 2011.
"Affectionately dubbed 'the Guru', Molly was the heartbeat, the champion and the spirit of Australian music," a statement from Meldrum's family said.
Among his most famous interviews was a 1977 sit-down with King Charles, in which Meldrum could not calm his jitters.
He stumbled over his lines, declaring: "Your Royal Highness... Oh, oh, I'm sweating like a pig".
King Charles reflected on the infamous interview for Countdown's 40th anniversary special, saying: "There is an old showbusiness saying which warns never to work with animals or children. But nobody prepared me for Molly Meldrum".
On Monday, an aide to the King said he had been "deeply saddened" to hear of Meldrum's death.
"His Majesty's interview with Molly is a moment he and many others will never forget - he hopes that interview will once again raise a few smiles as Australians honour Molly's legacy as a true giant of the music industry."
Elton John - a friend and regular interviewee - paid tribute to him as "an Australian legend and an institution", while pop star Kylie Minogue said she would be turning up the music in his honour.
"As a kid, I watched Molly Meldrum on Countdown every single weekend, in awe of the show and the magic it brought to our little TV in the lounge room."
"He championed so many Aussie artists and welcomed international artists to Australia in his own wonderful and inimitable way. I'm so grateful for his unwavering love and support."
Australia's Arts Minister Tony Burke said the country had lost an icon: "One of his greatest legacies will be the generations of Australians who grew up with his unmistakable enthusiasm and love of music."

WHY DECLARE
Start with the obvious objection. AI writes most code now, and it is best at the languages it has seen the most — so the sensible move is to use whatever has the biggest corpus and let the model figure it out. By that logic the era of new programming languages is over.
That argument gets its facts right and its conclusion backwards. Writing code is now nearly free; trusting it costs what it always did. An AI writing React verifies its work by resemblance — this looks like the billion lines it trained on — and resemblance is not correctness. Meanwhile less and less code passes under human eyes, which leaves the language and its compiler as the one reviewer that is always present. Handing the writing to a machine doesn’t make the language irrelevant. It makes it load-bearing.
Declare set out to be two things at once.
Expressive.A language that can say what a real interface is — not just data entry screens, but fast, polished, custom software designed to be used, even enjoyed: views that become the next view, motion that carries meaning, layouts that answer to content and to the screen they are on.
Verifiable.A language that can be learned, written, debugged and tested by an AI, and whose programs a compiler can check rather than guess at.
Most attempts to make code safe for machines make it duller for people. Declare refuses that tradeoff. Every feature that makes a program checkable — one tree for structure, style and behavior; every dependency visible to the compiler; one decider for each value — is also what makes it short, and readable to the person who has to judge it.
A well-designed experience is a set of decisions — how it should look, how it should move, what should feel inevitable — and those decisions are yours. An AI can produce a standard-looking app easily, and in Declare it can produce one verifiably. What it cannot supply is a custom-crafted design.
That is why layout, motion, states, theming and drawing are part of the language itself rather than libraries: aSpringon an attribute, a layout as a value a view holds, a mode as a state you are in or not. The continuous version of an interface is often less code than the discrete one. And because a Declare program is one complete description — no separate stylesheet, no framework lifecycle, no build of a dozen files — the design you meant is written plainly in the code, where you, a colleague or an AI can read it back and see that it is still what you meant.
What an AI gets from a mainstream stack is corpus leverage: fluency by imitation — broad, shallow, self-contradictory, unverifiable. The other kind is comprehension leverage: a language small enough to hand to a model whole, regular enough that its programs can be analyzed rather than pattern-matched, and backed by a compiler that turns each mistake into a precise correction. Corpus leverage arrives free with popularity. Comprehension leverage has to be designed in, and it is the only kind a new language can compete on.
It is a measured bet: a small language handed to a model in context has beaten the same model writing Python (study →), and a compiler that explains its errors measurably improves a model’s repairs (study →).
Declare was built the same way it is meant to be used: eval by eval. An agent that had never seen the language was given a written application spec and the Declare download, and built the app while I watched — how long it took, what it tripped on, what it found missing, how well its code read, how well the app worked. Another agent built the same spec in React. Over a hundred runs, what improved was not the model but the language: the same ticket-buying app went from 48 minutes to 24, compiler errors per build from 32 to 6. In the latest pair the Declare app was 1,279 lines to React’s 2,666, and its first build that ran passed all eleven hidden checks; React’s passed six. Single runs, not yet a benchmark.The runs, in full →
The most prized quality of a great interface — the continuity you feel in the best native apps — has always been bespoke: specialist craft, one interaction at a time, locked to a platform, and wrong in ways nothing catches. Declare makes that continuity the grain of the language, and puts it where a compiler can check it. The calendar is the proof: four views as one zooming surface, about 600 lines, human-designed and directed, and built with AI.
There is another generation of experiences beyond today’s hand-crafted best — built on a foundation with continuity at its core, deployed as widely as a URL, and shaped by people with an idea of how software should feel, working with an AI at their side. Declare is built to find out what they make.
Further:the FAQ·how it works·the whole language, in one file
WHERE THIS CAME FROM
I co-founded Laszlo Systems and led the team behind OpenLaszlo — a declarative UI language, first shipped in 2002, that pushed right to the edge of what that era’s web browsers could handle.
What brought me back to UI development wasMesa, a zoomable canvas app I built without using a browser framework, toolkit, or higher-level language. Mesa renders a thousand live objects at a 60fps floor, even on a phone. It’s been positively amazing to see how fast today’s browsers have become — and how powerful and flexible today’s web platform is.
And yet the web as it actually stands is still, mostly, slow and clunky. Even brand-new sites. How can that be?
It turns out the browser isn’t what makes the web feel worse than a good native app. It’s what we’ve built on top of it. A lot of accumulated code — and a lot of accumulated habits — take their toll, and the interfaces that do escape them are hand-crafted, one at a time, by specialists.
In June I handed the original OpenLaszlo compiler to an LLM and got back a modern port that compiles any OpenLaszlo program perfectly, byte-for-byte.
Seeing those programs again through fresh eyes — and seeing how small and how fast the sites built with them are — I decided the language deserved to be modernized. Declare is what came out of that: a direct descendant of OpenLaszlo, with the core ideas intact, built on an entirely new foundation, and shaped to be written with an LLM.
Enjoy!
— David Temkin

THE LANGUAGE
Declare is a language for building application interfaces. This file is the language: every form the grammar accepts and every rule the compiler enforces. The compiler completes it — every error carries a code, a position, and the rewrite that resolves it (§12), so nothing here needs to enumerate edge cases.
Declare is new, and no LLM has been trained on it. It resembles React, CSS, and HTML in places, and this file is where those resemblances stop. Every complete program below is compiled by the test suite, so the examples are current by construction; where this file and the compiler disagree, the compiler is right.
The classes and their attributes are in the reference —npx declare-help <name>answers any of them by name. How to work with Declare, and where everything else is, starts atskill/SKILL.md.
One boundary makes the rest of this file readable.Every capitalized tag is a class—View,Text, andImage, but equallyDataset,State,Spring, andKeyListener. The language is the grammar that declares, instantiates, configures, and relates them, and that grammar is what follows.
A Declare program is a tree of nodes whose attributes are related to each other by standing expressions the runtime keeps true.
A constraint is a relationship, not a callback.Read a reactive value inside one and you are subscribed to it; assign to that value and everything that reads it updates. There is no re-render, no diffing, no dependency array, and no hook, because nothing was ever a render.
Click the button and the label updates; resize the window and it stays centered. You wrote no update logic for either, and there is nowhere to put any. Every section below is this same idea applied to structure, space, data, style, and time.
Two brackets carry the entire syntax.[ … ]holds a node's members— attributes, declarations, methods, children — and the bracket nestingisthe tree.{ … }is TypeScript, type-checked against every class's real API.
An attribute's value takes four forms, and the spelling tells you which:
A bare literal is the value itself, so a name isnotone:fill = accentfails as a bare value. Reach a named value through braces —fill = { provided("theme").accent }.
Bare values have a small literal vocabulary the compiler owns: Lengths (100%), colors (navy,#336699), and keywords (center,x). Inside{ }none of it exists. You are in plain TypeScript, an identifier means what TypeScript says it means, and the compiler never reinterprets it.
A body is TypeScript, written as TypeScript writes it: ternaries, template literals, array chains, closures, casts (x as T,x!), annotations on locals and parameters, generics, and a method body's owntype,interface,enumandclassdeclarations. Everything type-level is checked, then stripped; what TypeScript compiles (an enum, a class's parameter properties), the compiler compiles. One limit, a compile error naming the rewrite:a value body is a single expression— statements live in methods.
A:pathmay also appear inside a{ }body, and this is central rather than exotic: it is how anything conditional over replicated data gets written.text = { :on ? :title : "—" }reads the datapath exactly as the bare form does, then computes with it in TypeScript. Read{ }as "TypeScript, plus datapath reads."
Two lexical notes. A"…"string ends at its line, in a bare value as in a{ }body; a"""block is the form for long text. And aDataset's literal body is strict JSON (§7) — the one place{ }is not TypeScript at all.
Everything inside[ ]is a member, in one of five shapes. Two of them look nearly identical and mean different things.
Any view can paint itself by definingdraw(d: DrawContext)— graphs, gauges, iconography, marks no fill or font gives you. It is an ordinary method:Viewcalls it from a constraint of its own (drawing = { record(draw) }), so it runs on invalidation and re-runs when what it read changes, never per frame — the same rule as any method a constraint calls.dtakes the Canvas2D drawing calls (fillStyle,beginPath,moveTo,stroke, …); what it records, every renderer paints.
name = valuesets an attribute that exists;name: Type = valuedeclares a new one.Declaring is how reactive state enters a program; setting is how it is wired. A declaration's type is a TypeScript type —number,string[],"idle" | "busy",Map<string, Row>,{ x: number; y: number },[number, number],(id: string) => void,Row | null— naming TypeScript's built-ins, Declare's own (Color,Length, …), your classes, your schemas (§7), or a type ascriptblock declares;object/arraystand for a record or list of no declared shape, in a cast too.T?is Declare's shorthand forT | null, and takes?.'sundefinedasnull. A type that a declaration cannot hold in place (a conditional or template-literal type) is named once in ascriptblock and used by name. The one place a type meets the member syntax is a[after it: glued and empty it is an array (w: Window[]); after a space it opens a named child (w: Window [ … ]).

Declare is a programming language for user interfaces — a domain-specific language, the way SQL is a domain-specific language for querying data. You describe an interface as a tree of views with attributes; any attribute can be a live expression, and when the things it reads change, everything that depends on it updates. All real logic is ordinary TypeScript. Programs compile in the browser or ahead of time, and one program renders to the DOM, directly to pixels on a canvas, or as a native Mac app.
Because most of what makes UI code hard isn't your application — it's the plumbing. In Declare there is no render lifecycle to manage, no state synchronization to orchestrate, no CSS cascade to fight, no build pipeline to configure. An application is a readable tree of declarations: the flagship calendar — four views, continuous zoom, drag-to-reschedule — is about 600 lines of code you can read end to end. Given the same brief, an agent's Declare app came out at half the code of its React app. And Declare is built for the era when much code is written by machines: the language is small enough to hand a model in its entirety, and strict enough to verify what comes back.
Declare is at its best where an interface has to be designed, not just assembled: custom, fluid experiences of the kind you find in the best native apps — calendars, editors, dashboards, product sites — where views become one another and motion carries meaning. Everyday apps come with it: forms, lists, settings screens and admin tools are what the library's controls are for, and content-heavy apps work well (Markdown rendering is built in). Everything on this site is a Declare program: the homepage, the documentation, the calendar, the desktop.
An AI can produce a standard-looking app easily, and in Declare it can produce one verifiably. A custom experience is a set of decisions — how it should look, how it should move, what should happen when — and those come from human judgment and direction. What Declare changes is how directly those decisions can be expressed in code: layout, motion, states and theming are the language itself, so what you meant stays legible in the code, and the AI that writes it, the compiler that checks it and the colleague who reads it later are all looking at the same design.
Yes, with effort. Windows that drag, resize and layer; minimizing into live thumbnails; a magnifying dock; menus that follow focus; other programs running inside windows — in a mainstream web stack each of those is usually its own library or its own project, and keeping them coherent (focus, stacking, hit-testing, animation that can be interrupted) is where the effort goes. In Declare they are the language and its library, and thedesktopis one program of 2,011 lines of code. That is why it makes a good acid test for any UI toolkit.

It's a language, not a framework inside JavaScript. In React and its relatives, the UI is a function you re-run — the framework diffs the output and patches the page, and you manage the machinery (hooks, memoization, effects) that keeps re-running affordable. In Declare, the UI is astanding structure: values flow through it when things change, and nothing re-renders because nothing was ever a render. There is also no HTML/CSS/JS trinity — structure, style, and behavior are one tree in one language. Its nearest relatives are declarative-tree systems like SwiftUI and QML, but Declare is web-native, compiled, renderer-independent, and uses TypeScript — not a new scripting dialect — for logic.
The compiler parses the declarations, statically extracts every constraint's dependencies, type-checks every{ }body as real TypeScript against every class's typed API, resolves the components you use (the standard library auto-includes by name), and emits a self-contained program. The benefits: errors surface before the program runs, with messages that name the fix; reactivity isderived by the compiler, not guessed at runtime, so behavior is predictable and analyzable by tools; production output is small; and programs are data — the same compiler powers the documentation system, static extraction for crawlers, and live editing. The compiler itself runs anywhere — in Node, or in the browser.
The[ ]structure is Declare; everything inside{ }— expressions, event handlers, methods — is ordinary TypeScript, type-checked with full knowledge of every class's attributes. There is no new expression language to learn. The declarative layer contributes structure and reactivity; TypeScript contributes logic — and everything you (or your model) already know about it carries over.

Declare is a from-the-ground-up modern successor to OpenLaszlo, the open-source rich-internet-application platform first released in 2002. OpenLaszlo had the core ideas remarkably early: interfaces declared as trees, attributes connected by live constraints, declarative data binding, compiled applications running in the browser — a decade before today's declarative frameworks. Declare  keeps those convictions — the declarative tree, constraint-based reactivity, a real compiler — while rebuilding everything else for the modern era: a clean keyword-free syntax, TypeScript for logic, DOM and canvas renderers, in-browser compilation, and a design shaped from day one for the LLM era.

Declare · runtime architecture
A Declare front end is one self-contained artifact — small enough to hold in your head, strict enough for a machine to verify, rich enough for an ambitious application. This is what Declare’s runtime does to make that true.
Declare asks you to believe something unusual about an application’s front end: that it is complete. Everything the interface does — where each box goes, how a paragraph wraps, what a click landed on, how a view becomes the next one — is written in the one program, as relationships rather than steps, so a machine can verify it and a person can read it. That puts a demand on what runs underneath: if the browser decided the layout, or the DOM routed the click, the program would not be complete. So the runtime makes those decisions itself, once, and hands the browser what it does best.

ASpringis an attribute with a target; each frame it writes its next value, and that write is a settle like any other. Nothing about animation is special-cased, so a new target mid-flight is simply the next write: the spring retargets from wherever it is, and everything that read it follows. Interruptibility isn’t a feature of an animation system; it is what a reactive graph does when you write to it.
Every box is decided before the host hears of it — by arithmetic over attributes, by a layout (a class with one method,place()), or by the content’s own size. Text is the one place the host contributes a number, the width of a glyph; wrapping and height are the runtime’s, so a paragraph breaks into the same lines on every renderer. Because the runtime placed every box, it also answers the inverse question — what is under this point — and that one answer decides hover, press, and where a drag lands.
04
Because the compiler hands over the whole graph up front, the runtime doesn’t have to discover anything as it runs. Its reactive core (the graph, the settle, and the arithmetic of layout, springs and visibility) is a small C kernel: WebAssembly in the browser, linked natively on the Mac. Bodies that are plain arithmetic arrive as bytecode the kernel evaluates itself, without returning to JavaScript.
Moving the core there cut update time by 42–53% on every platform measured (Chrome, iOS Safari and the Mac host), and a window drag’s by 81–93%. The rules evaluated didn’t change; each one simply costs less.

Everything above happens on one side of a single interface,Surface— 71 methods such assetX,setFillandsetTextthat the runtime calls and a backend implements. script.intro: Guten Morgen und herzlich willkommen zu Ihren Nachrichten. Heute blicken wir auf die aktuelle Lage in der Tech-Welt, die geopolitischen Spannungen und natürlich auf die Umweltauswirkungen von Konflikten. Aber zuerst gibt es eine große Story aus dem Silicon Valley.

segments.headline: Trump erzielt 'Deal' zur Wiedereinsetzung von Nvidia-CEO Jensen Huang inmitten von Spionagevorwürfen
segments.narration: Der ehemalige US-Präsident Donald Trump hat laut eigener Aussage eine entscheidende Rolle bei der Wiedereinsetzung von Nvidia-CEO Jensen Huang gespielt. Huang war wegen angeblicher Affären, darunter eine mit einer mutmaßlichen chinesischen Spionin, zurückgetreten. Trump behauptet, er habe den Vorstand von Nvidia 'überzeugt', Huang zurückzuholen, um weitere Kursverluste zu verhindern. Diese Entscheidung stößt jedoch auf parteiübergreifende Kritik von US-Abgeordneten, die nationale Sicherheitsbedenken äußern und eine umfassende Untersuchung fordern. Nächste Woche soll Huang vor dem Kongress aussagen.
segments.summary_short: Donald Trump beansprucht die Wiedereinsetzung von Nvidia-CEO Jensen Huang für sich, der nach Vorwürfen einer Spionageaffäre zurückgetreten war, was jedoch parteiübergreifende Kritik hervorruft.

segments.headline: NATO-Chef warnt vor Weltraumbedrohung nach Berichten über russische Atomwaffen im All
segments.narration: Inmitten von Geheimdienstberichten über russische Pläne zum Start eines nuklear bestückten Satelliten ins All hat NATO-Chef Mark Rutte bekräftigt, dass die Allianz jeden Zentimeter ihres Territoriums verteidigen wird, was auch den Weltraum einschließt. Obwohl Russland diese Vorwürfe als 'unbegründete Anschuldigungen' zurückweist, äußerten sowohl Rutte als auch Bundeskanzler Merz tiefe Besorgnis. Deutschland mahnt dabei zur Besonnenheit, während die NATO ihre Verteidigungsstrategien überprüft. Gleichzeitig kündigte Bundesverteidigungsminister Boris Pistorius an, dass Deutschland künftig ukrainische Aufklärungsdrohnen vom Typ 'Babka' hierzulande herstellen wird, um die militärstrategische Zusammenarbeit mit der Ukraine zu stärken. Zudem soll das ukrainische Gefechtsführungssystem 'Delta' weiterentwickelt und von der Bundeswehr genutzt werden.
segments.summary_short: NATO-Chef Rutte verspricht Verteidigung im Weltraum angesichts russischer Atomwaffenberichte, während Deutschland die militärische Zusammenarbeit mit der Ukraine durch Drohnenproduktion und Systementwicklung ausbaut.

segments.headline: Südkorea meldet erneut russische Militärflugzeuge in Luftverteidigungszone
segments.narration: Ganz woanders, vor der Küste Südkoreas, gab es erneut Meldungen über russische Militärflugzeuge. Laut südkoreanischen Sicherheitsbehörden sind am Dienstagmorgen mehrere russische Maschinen in die Luftverteidigungszone um die Insel Ulleung eingedrungen. Südkoreanische Kampfflugzeuge stiegen zur Abwehr auf, woraufhin die russischen Jets abzogen. Solche Vorfälle mit russischen Militärflugzeugen wurden in letzter Zeit auch von Taiwan und Japan gemeldet. Eine anfängliche Warnung in Südkorea sprach fälschlicherweise von einem 'mutmaßlich nordkoreanischen Flugzeug', was laut Medienberichten auf einen unbeabsichtigten Textbaustein zurückzuführen ist.
segments.summary_short: Südkorea meldet, dass russische Militärflugzeuge erneut in seine Luftverteidigungszone eingedrungen sind, was zu einem Abfangeinsatz südkoreanischer Kampfjets führte.

segments.headline: Verseuchtes Wasser und Gift in Trümmern: Kriegsfolgen im Gazastreifen bedrohen Generationen
segments.narration: Ein trauriges Thema, das uns lange beschäftigen wird, sind die Kriegsfolgen im Gazastreifen. Dort leidet die Bevölkerung massiv unter verseuchtem Wasser und giftigen Trümmern. Laut der Hilfsorganisation Oxfam sind vier Fünftel der Abwasserpumpstationen zerstört, was dazu führt, dass täglich Tausende Kubikmeter ungeklärtes Abwasser ins Meer und in den Boden gelangen. Dies führt zu einer dramatischen Zunahme von Krankheiten, insbesondere bei Kindern. Labordaten zeigen eine massive Verunreinigung des Grundwassers mit Kolibakterien. Zudem sind über 60 Millionen Tonnen Trümmer mit Asbest, Dioxinen und Sprengstoffrückständen kontaminiert. Oxfam spricht von 'Umwelt-Kriegsverbrechen', deren Auswirkungen noch Jahrzehnte spürbar sein werden und ganze Generationen bedrohen.
segments.summary_short: Im Gazastreifen führen zerstörte Infrastruktur und tonnenweise kontaminierte Trümmer zu massivem Leid durch verseuchtes Wasser und giftige Stoffe, was langanhaltende Gesundheits- und Umweltprobleme verursacht.

segments.headline: Juncts: Eine DM-Inbox für fünf KI-Apps mit Claude und ChatGPT
segments.narration: Kommen wir zu einer spannenden Neuerung aus der Tech-Welt: 'Juncts' wurde vorgestellt. Das ist im Grunde eine zentrale Inbox für Direktnachrichten, die es Nutzern ermöglicht, mit fünf verschiedenen Apps zu interagieren, in denen wiederum Claude und ChatGPT integriert sind. Ein 'Show HN'-Projekt, das auf Hacker News für Aufmerksamkeit sorgt.
segments.summary_short: Juncts ist eine neue DM-Inbox, die die Interaktion mit fünf KI-Apps, darunter Claude und ChatGPT, in einem einzigen Interface ermöglicht.

segments.headline: Heizkörper hacken: Ein Hobbyprojekt für Smart-Home-Fans
segments.narration: Bleiben wir gleich bei technologischen Spielereien, aber im privaten Bereich. Ein Bastler namens Q. Santos hat seine elektrischen Heizkörper per Funk gehackt, um sie zentral zu steuern. Ursprünglich wollte er nur seinen alten Fernseher mit einem selbstgebauten IR-Sender 'smart genug' machen, damit er ihn von der Couch aus bedienen kann. Mit Hilfe von KI hat er dann das Funkprotokoll seiner Heizkörper entschlüsselt und kann diese jetzt sogar per Handy steuern – das alles 'zum Spaß und ohne Gewinnabsicht'. Ein tolles Beispiel für 'Smart Home Hacking' für jedermann.
segments.summary_short: Ein Entwickler hat seine Funk-Heizkörper gehackt, um sie mit Hilfe von KI zentral und ferngesteuert bedienen zu können, nachdem er bereits seinen Fernseher smart gemacht hatte.

segments.headline: Declare: Eine neue UI-Sprache für Menschen und KI
segments.narration: Eine weitere spannende Entwicklung im Bereich Softwareentwicklung ist die Vorstellung von 'Declare'. Das ist eine neue domänenspezifische Sprache, die speziell für die Entwicklung von Benutzeroberflächen konzipiert wurde. Der Clou: Sie ist sowohl für menschliche Entwickler als auch für künstliche Intelligenzen optimiert. Die Idee dahinter ist, dass KI zwar viel Code schreiben kann, aber die Überprüfbarkeit und Korrektheit oft zu wünschen übrig lässt. Declare soll hier Abhilfe schaffen, indem sie eine kompakte, präzise und überprüfbare Syntax bietet, die es ermöglicht, auch komplexe und flüssige UI-Erlebnisse effizient zu gestalten.
segments.summary_short: Declare ist eine neue domänenspezifische Sprache für Benutzeroberflächen, die entwickelt wurde, um die Erstellung und Verifizierung von UI-Code für Menschen und KI zu optimieren.

segments.headline: Deutscher Dokumentarfilm 'Der talentierte Mr. F.' gewinnt Internationalen Emmy
segments.narration: Zum Schluss noch eine gute Nachricht aus der Kultur: Deutsche Dokumentarfilmer haben einen Internationalen Emmy gewonnen. Ihre ARD-Produktion 'Der talentierte Mr. F.' wurde in New York City in der Kategorie 'Arts Programming' ausgezeichnet. Der Film erzählt die unglaubliche Geschichte von zwei jungen Filmemachern, die auf die Jagd nach einem Mann gehen, der ihren Animationsfilm gestohlen und damit Preise gewonnen hat. Ein Mix aus True Crime und Roadmovie, der die Jury offenbar überzeugt hat.
segments.summary_short: Die deutsche ARD-Dokumentation 'Der talentierte Mr. F.', die die Geschichte eines Filmdiebstahls erzählt, hat einen Internationalen Emmy in der Kategorie 'Arts Programming' gewonnen.
